"title": "Stem Cell Microarrays for Assessing Growth Factor Signaling in Engineered Glycan Microenvironments",
"authors": "Glycan Microenvironments (University of California San Diego); Austen L Michalak (University of California San Diego); Greg W Trieger (University of California San Diego); Kelsey A Trieger (University of California San Diego); Kamil Godula (University of California San Diego)",

"executive_summary": "This study introduces a stem cell microarray platform that integrates glycosaminoglycan (GAG) polysaccharides into a polyacrylamide hydrogel to directly measure their contributions to growth factor (GF) signaling in cells. The motivation stems from the essential regulatory role of extracellular glycans, such as heparan sulfate (HS), in establishing gradients of morphogens and forming active signaling complexes at the cell surface, yet their structural complexity and compositional heterogeneity make structure-function relationships difficult to establish. Recent advances in synthetic, recombinant, and chemoenzymatic technologies now enable the production of well-defined GAG structures, creating an opportunity to systematically analyze both GF binding and signaling. The platform arrays HS-protein conjugates on polyacrylamide hydrogels to generate stable ECM-mimetic microenvironments capable of binding FGF2 and influencing embryonic stem cell (ESC) signaling. The selectivity of FGF2 binding and activity is defined by the chemical composition of the HS polysaccharides. The study uses murine ESCs lacking Exostosin 1 (Ext1 -/-), which lack cell surface HS and cannot engage HS-dependent GFs like FGF2, to isolate the effects of arrayed GAGs. The MAPK pathway activation in response to FGF2 is quantified via immunofluorescence for phosphorylated ERK1/2 (pERK) and total ERK1/2 (ERK). Key findings include the demonstration that covalently linked heparin provides superior FGF2 binding capacity (~5-to 10-fold higher signal) compared to non-covalently immobilized heparin, and that heparin arrays remain stable with ~40% of FGF2 binding activity retained after 48 hours under cellular culture conditions. The study confirms that NHS-crosslinking enhances the stability of GAG displays without altering protein binding specificity, and that Ext1 -/-ESCs stimulated with FGF2 in the presence of immobilized or soluble heparin show significant increases in ERK1/2 phosphorylation. This platform offers a convenient tool to systematically analyze the biological activities of extracellular GAGs in stem cell signaling and to accelerate the development of new bioactive glycomaterials for stem cell-based therapeutic applications.",

summary.title: Stem Cell Microarrays for Assessing Growth Factor Signaling in Engineered Glycan Microenvironments
summary.authors: Glycan Microenvironments (University of California San Diego); Austen L Michalak (University of California San Diego); Greg W Trieger (University of California San Diego); Kelsey A Trieger (University of California San Diego); Kamil Godula (University of California San Diego)
summary.field_subfield: Chemical Biology / Biomaterials for Regenerative Medicine
summary.executive_summary: This study introduces a stem cell microarray platform that integrates glycosaminoglycan (GAG) polysaccharides into a polyacrylamide hydrogel to directly measure their contributions to growth factor (GF) signaling in cells. The motivation stems from the essential regulatory role of extracellular glycans, such as heparan sulfate (HS), in establishing gradients of morphogens and forming active signaling complexes at the cell surface, yet their structural complexity and compositional heterogeneity make structure-function relationships difficult to establish. Recent advances in synthetic, recombinant, and chemoenzymatic technologies now enable the production of well-defined GAG structures, creating an opportunity to systematically analyze both GF binding and signaling. The platform arrays HS-protein conjugates on polyacrylamide hydrogels to generate stable ECM-mimetic microenvironments capable of binding FGF2 and influencing embryonic stem cell (ESC) signaling. The selectivity of FGF2 binding and activity is defined by the chemical composition of the HS polysaccharides. The study uses murine ESCs lacking Exostosin 1 (Ext1 -/-), which lack cell surface HS and cannot engage HS-dependent GFs like FGF2, to isolate the effects of arrayed GAGs. The MAPK pathway activation in response to FGF2 is quantified via immunofluorescence for phosphorylated ERK1/2 (pERK) and total ERK1/2 (ERK). Key findings include the demonstration that covalently linked heparin provides superior FGF2 binding capacity (~5-to 10-fold higher signal) compared to non-covalently immobilized heparin, and that heparin arrays remain stable with ~40% of FGF2 binding activity retained after 48 hours under cellular culture conditions. The study confirms that NHS-crosslinking enhances the stability of GAG displays without altering protein binding specificity, and that Ext1 -/-ESCs stimulated with FGF2 in the presence of immobilized or soluble heparin show significant increases in ERK1/2 phosphorylation. This platform offers a convenient tool to systematically analyze the biological activities of extracellular GAGs in stem cell signaling and to accelerate the development of new bioactive glycomaterials for stem cell-based therapeutic applications.

Executive Summary
This study introduces a stem cell microarray platform that integrates glycosaminoglycan (GAG) polysaccharides into a polyacrylamide hydrogel to directly measure their contributions to growth factor (GF) signaling in cells. The motivation stems from the essential regulatory role of extracellular glycans, such as heparan sulfate (HS), in establishing gradients of morphogens and forming active signaling complexes at the cell surface, yet their structural complexity and compositional heterogeneity make structure-function relationships difficult to establish. Recent advances in synthetic, recombinant, and chemoenzymatic technologies now enable the production of well-defined GAG structures, creating an opportunity to systematically analyze both GF binding and signaling. The platform arrays HS-protein conjugates on polyacrylamide hydrogels to generate stable ECM-mimetic microenvironments capable of binding FGF2 and influencing embryonic stem cell (ESC) signaling. The selectivity of FGF2 binding and activity is defined by the chemical composition of the HS polysaccharides. The study uses murine ESCs lacking Exostosin 1 (Ext1 -/-), which lack cell surface HS and cannot engage HS-dependent GFs like FGF2, to isolate the effects of arrayed GAGs. The MAPK pathway activation in response to FGF2 is quantified via immunofluorescence for phosphorylated ERK1/2 (pERK) and total ERK1/2 (ERK). Key findings include the demonstration that covalently linked heparin provides superior FGF2 binding capacity (~5-to 10-fold higher signal) compared to non-covalently immobilized heparin, and that heparin arrays remain stable with ~40% of FGF2 binding activity retained after 48 hours under cellular culture conditions. The study confirms that NHS-crosslinking enhances the stability of GAG displays without altering protein binding specificity, and that Ext1 -/-ESCs stimulated with FGF2 in the presence of immobilized or soluble heparin show significant increases in ERK1/2 phosphorylation. This platform offers a convenient tool to systematically analyze the biological activities of extracellular GAGs in stem cell signaling and to accelerate the development of new bioactive glycomaterials for stem cell-based therapeutic applications.

Research Context
Extracellular glycans like GAGs are essential regulators of growth factor signaling. GAGs harbor binding sites for growth factors and establish signaling gradients. GAGs promote formation of active signaling complexes at the cell surface. GAGs are pursued as biologically active components for regenerative biomaterials. Structural complexity hinders structure-function analysis of GAGs. HS polysaccharides are essential regulators of GF signaling. HS comprise chains of alternating residues with sequential modifications. Recent advances enable production of well-defined GAG structures. Arrays of HS structures are used to profile HS-binding protein specificity. Multiplexed on-array analysis of HS-dependent signaling could streamline biomaterial discovery.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether GAGs can be arrayed to measure their contributions to GF signaling. The hypothesis is that GAG polysaccharides conjugated to adhesion proteins can be introduced into hydrogels to measure signaling. The platform should enable analysis of both GF binding and signaling in response to GAGs. The hypothesis is that FGF2 binding and activity are defined by the chemical composition of HS. The hypothesis is that Ext1 -/-ESCs isolate the effects of arrayed GAGs on FGF2 signaling. The hypothesis is that covalent crosslinking enhances GAG retention without altering binding specificity. The hypothesis is that immobilized GAGs can facilitate GF-mediated activation of signaling events. The predicted outcome is that well-defined GAG structures enable systematic structure-function analysis.

Methodological Details
The study used murine embryonic stem cells lacking Exostosin 1 expression. Ext1 -/-ESCs lack cell surface HS structures and cannot engage HS-dependent GFs. The cell model was chosen to isolate the effects of arrayed GAGs on FGF2 signaling. Several surface passivation strategies were screened for array construction. A thin poly(acrylamide) hydrogel deposited on glass best supported ESC growth. The hydrogel method followed a protocol by Brafman et al. Gelatin was loaded into the hydrogel in its dehydrated form. Gelatin was spotted at a concentration of 500 µg/mL in PBS. Best ESC growth was observed over 6 days in culture. Heparin (12 kDa) was used as a model HS glycan. Heparin concentrations ranged from 50 to 750 µg/mL. Heparin was crosslinked via carboxylic acid groups activated as NHS esters. Heparin was activated with EDC in HEPES buffer at pH 7.4. The coupling reagent EDC was used at 4°C for 18 hours. Purification was performed by size exclusion on a PD10 column. Low levels of crosslinking were targeted at ~15% carboxylic acid crosslinks per chain. A panel of CS, DS, and HA GAGs was arrayed. Heparin was chemically treated to remove 6-O-, 2-O-, and N-sulfates. N-desulfated heparin had amino groups capped as acetamides. The array was probed with FGF2, CS56, and HABP. FGF2 was labeled with AlexaFluor 647. Slides were washed for 3 hours prior to staining. Cells were seeded at an intermediary density of 40,000 cells/cm². Cells were grown for 24 hours in embryonic culture media with LIF and FBS. The last 24 hours were carried out under serum-free conditions. Oct4 was used as an embryonic marker. Nestin was used as a neural differentiation marker. Cells were stimulated with FGF2 at 0.5 ng/mL for 15 min at 37°C. MAPK activity was quantified using antibodies against Erk1/2 and pErk1/2. A microarrays scanner was used to detect fluorescence. Image J analysis was used to confirm co-localization of pERK and ERK signals. Soluble heparin (s-Hep, 5 µg/mL) was used as a positive control.

Procedures And Architectures
The platform integrates GAG-protein conjugates into a hydrogel-supported stem cell microarray. The goal was to analyze the activity of extracellular glycans in growth factor signaling. The platform enables rapid development and optimization of functional glycomaterials. GAGs harbor binding sites for a range of growth factors and morphogens. GAGs help establish gradients of molecules in the extracellular matrix. The platform arrays HS-protein conjugates on polyacrylamide hydrogels. The arrays generate stable ECM-mimetic microenvironments. The microenvironments can influence ESC signaling. Covalent crosslinking facilitated retention of polysaccharides during cell culture. Crosslinking did not alter the protein-binding specificity of the polysaccharides. The arrays were generated by printing and physisorption of GAG polysaccharides. GAG polysaccharides were crosslinked with extracellular matrix proteins. The immobilized GAG structures facilitated GF-mediated activation of signaling events. Signaling events were detected and quantified using immunofluorescence. The platform offers a convenient tool to systematically analyze GAG biological activities. The platform accelerates development of new bioactive glycomaterials. The platform capitalizes on the expanding repertoire of synthetic GAG structures. The study leverages synthetic, recombinant, and chemoenzymatic GAG technologies. The platform supports the discovery and optimization of new biomaterials. The platform is suitable for examining ECM protein components in hydrogels.

Key Results
Covalently linked heparin showed superior FGF2 binding capacity. Covalently linked heparin provided ~5-to 10-fold higher signal. Non-covalently immobilized heparin showed lower FGF2 binding. FGF2 was retained on the array surface for 48 hours. Retention was assessed under cellular culture conditions at 37°C, 5% CO2. GAG molecular recognition and selectivity was assessed on the array. FGF2 binding showed greatest preference for fully sulfated heparin. 2O and 6O-sulfated heparin followed in preference. Removal of 6-O-, 2-O-, and N-sulfates resulted in progressive loss of activity. Loss of activity agreed with known requirements of 2-O- and N-sulfation. CS56 and HABP exhibited high specificity for CS and HA. NHS-crosslinking enhanced stability of GAG displays. Crosslinking did not alter protein binding specificity of the polysaccharides. Heparin arrays remained stable with ~40% of FGF2 binding activity after 48 hours. An initial decrease in binding activity occurred during the first 18 hours. Ext1 -/-ESCs were chosen as the cell model. Ext1 -/-ESCs lack cell surface HS structures. Ext1 -/-ESCs are unable to engage a range of HS-dependent GFs. Ext1 -/-ESCs cannot engage FGF2. Too sparse seeding (20,000 cells/cm²) resulted in slow growth. Too high seeding density (100,000 cells/cm²) led to rapid proliferation. Intermediary seeding density (40,000 cells/cm²) produced consistent monolayers. Monolayers retained high levels of Oct4 expression. Monolayers showed no obvious signs of differentiation. MAPK pathway activation was examined in response to FGF2. The signaling response is accompanied by changes in phosphorylation of Erk1/2. Ext1 -/-ESCs were seeded on spots with gelatin with or without NHS-crosslinked heparin. Cells were grown for 48 hours under optimized culture and starvation conditions. ERK1/2 protein levels were similar across all conditions. Only Ext1 -/-ESCs stimulated with FGF2 in the presence of heparin showed significant increase in Erk1/2 phosphorylation. Lower MAPK activity was observed on arrayed heparin compared to soluble form. Lower activity may be due to limited accessibility of immobilized heparin. Immobilized heparin was accessible to only a subset of FGFRs. FGF2 stimulation showed heparin dose-responsive ERK1/2 phosphorylation. The positive control soluble heparin restored MAPK activity in Ext1 -/-ESCs.
